theory.what: OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) is a link-state routing protocol standardized as RFC 2328. Unlike distance-vector protocols (RIP, EIGRP) that share full routing tables with neighbours, OSPF floods Link-State Advertisements (LSAs) to all routers in an area, building a complete topological map called the Link-State Database (LSDB). Every OSPF router then runs Dijkstra's Shortest Path First (SPF) algorithm independently on that LSDB to compute the shortest path tree to every destination. The result is a loop-free, metric-based routing table where every router converges on the same topology picture. OSPF supports VLSM, CIDR, authentication (MD5/SHA), and classless routing natively. It uses cost as its metric, calculated as the reference bandwidth (100 Mbps by default) divided by the interface bandwidth, giving administrators fine-grained control over path selection.
theory.why: OSPF is the dominant interior gateway protocol (IGP) in enterprise and service provider networks for several reasons. First, its fast convergence: when a link fails, OSPF detects the change within seconds (Hello timer: 10s, Dead timer: 40s) and floods the update network-wide, triggering only affected routers to re-run SPF rather than recalculating everything. Second, its hierarchical design through areas dramatically reduces routing table size and SPF computation for larger networks — routers in Area 1 do not need to know every link in Area 2, only inter-area routes via the Area Border Router (ABR). Third, OSPF provides loop-free routing intrinsically: because every router has the complete topology (not just next-hop information), SPF cannot produce routing loops. Fourth, OSPF is vendor-interoperable, unlike Cisco's EIGRP, making it mandatory for multi-vendor environments. Fifth, LSA types enable advanced capabilities such as route summarization (Type 3 summary LSAs), external route injection (Type 5 AS-external LSAs from redistribution), and Not-So-Stubby-Area (NSSA) partial external injection (Type 7). Mastering OSPF is required for CCNA, CCNP, JNCIA, and virtually all network engineering certifications and roles.
theory.how: OSPF operation follows a structured five-phase process. Phase 1 — Neighbour Discovery: Routers send Hello packets every 10 seconds (default) to multicast 224.0.0.5 (AllSPFRouters) on broadcast media. The Hello packet contains the router ID, area ID, authentication data, subnet mask, Hello/Dead intervals, and neighbour list. For two routers to become neighbours, they must agree on: area ID, timers, authentication type, subnet mask, and stub area flag. Phase 2 — LSA Exchange: Once neighbours reach the 2-Way state (both have seen each other's Hello), they proceed through ExStart/Exchange states to compare their LSDB summaries using Database Description (DBD) packets. A designated router (DR) and backup designated router (BDR) are elected on broadcast networks to reduce LSA flooding from O(n²) to O(n). Phase 3 — Database Synchronisation: After identifying missing LSAs in the Exchange phase, routers send Link-State Request (LSR) packets and receive Link-State Update (LSU) packets in response. This continues until both databases are identical, reaching the Full adjacency state on multi-access networks. Phase 4 — SPF Computation: Each router independently runs Dijkstra's algorithm on its LSDB to construct a Shortest Path Tree with itself as root, then installs the best (lowest-cost) routes into the routing table. The SPF algorithm examines every link in the LSDB exactly once, producing a loop-free tree topology. Phase 5 — Ongoing Maintenance: Hello packets continue every 10 seconds to maintain adjacencies. If a router stops responding, the Dead timer (40s default) expires, the neighbour is declared Down, the originating router floods a new LSA with the failed link's new state, and all receiving routers re-run SPF for that portion of the topology. OSPF neighbour states in order: Down → Attempt (NBMA only) → Init → 2-Way → ExStart → Exchange → Loading → Full.
theory.when: Use OSPF in any network that needs fast convergence, hierarchical scaling, and vendor independence. Typical scenarios include: (1) Enterprise campus networks with dozens to hundreds of routers organised into a core (Area 0) and multiple leaf areas for departments, buildings, or geographic regions; (2) ISP backbone networks where OSPF runs within each AS supporting multiple routing domains; (3) Data centre leaf-spine topologies where OSPF over BGP provides underlay reachability; (4) Multi-vendor environments where a standardised, open protocol is mandatory; (5) MPLS LDP and TE environments where OSPF provides the IGP underlay. Use OSPF Area 0 for the backbone transit core, standard areas for leaf connectivity, stub areas to reduce LSA flooding at remote sites, and NSSA to inject limited external routes without receiving full external tables. Avoid OSPF in flat networks exceeding 500 routers within a single area (create areas), in networks with frequent flapping links (increase timers to 20/80), or when very rapid sub-second convergence is absolutely required (consider IS-IS with tuned timers instead).
key_concepts: Link-State vs Distance-Vector
Dijkstra SPF algorithm
Area hierarchy (Backbone Area 0, standard, stub, NSSA, totally stubby)
LSA Types 1-7 (Router, Network, Summary, ASBR-Summary, AS-External, NSSA)
DR/BDR election on broadcast networks (higher priority = preferred, highest RID as tiebreak)
Hello/Dead timers (10s/40s default on broadcast, 30s/120s on NBMA)
OSPF cost = 10⁸ / interface bandwidth (configurable via auto-cost reference-bandwidth)
Router ID (highest loopback IP, then highest physical IP)
ABR (Area Border Router) and ASBR (AS Boundary Router)
Virtual links for connecting discontinuous Area 0
OSPF authentication (MD5, SHA, null)
Passive interfaces suppress Hello transmissions on access links
Route summarisation on ABRs using area range
OSPFv3 for IPv6 (uses link-local addresses, runs per-link)
Graceful restart / NSF for hitless software upgrades
theory.configuration:
! Enable OSPF process 1 with manual Router-ID
router ospf 1
 router-id 1.1.1.1

! Advertise networks into specific areas
 network 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
 network 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 area 1
 network 172.16.0.0 0.0.255.255 area 2

! Suppress Hello on access-facing interfaces
 passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/0

! Set reference bandwidth for consistent cost calculation
 auto-cost reference-bandwidth 10000

! Summarise routes from Area 1 into Area 0
 area 1 range 192.168.0.0 255.255.0.0

! Configure Area 2 as a Totally Stubby area (default route only)
 area 2 stub no-summary

! Enable SPF throttling for faster convergence
 timers throttle spf 50 200 10000

! Set interface cost manually (overrides auto-cost)
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip ospf cost 10
 ip ospf hello-interval 10
 ip ospf dead-interval 40
 ip ospf priority 10
 ip ospf authentication message-digest
 ip ospf message-digest-key 1 md5 OSPFSecret123
troubleshooting: show ip ospf neighbor [detail] — Verify neighbours have reached Full state
show ip ospf database — Inspect LSDB contents per LSA type
show ip ospf interface [name] — Check timers, cost, state, DR/BDR
show ip route ospf — Verify OSPF-learned routes in RIB
show ip protocols — Confirm OSPF process configuration
show ip ospf — Display process ID, RID, SPF stats, areas
debug ip ospf adj — Troubleshoot neighbour adjacency issues in real time
debug ip ospf packet — Analyse incoming/outgoing OSPF packets
clear ip ospf process — Force full OSPF restart (use with caution!)

theory.what: BGP (Border Gateway Protocol), defined in RFC 4271, is the path-vector routing protocol that interconnects the autonomous systems (ASes) forming the global internet. Unlike IGPs (OSPF, EIGRP) that care about the lowest-cost path, BGP is a policy-driven protocol where operators select paths based on business relationships, traffic engineering goals, and administrative preferences expressed through path attributes. BGP operates over TCP (port 179), ensuring reliable incremental updates without the periodic full-table refreshes of earlier protocols. Each BGP route carries a set of attributes: AS_PATH (the list of AS numbers the route has traversed, used for loop detection and path length comparison), NEXT_HOP (the IP address of the next-hop router), LOCAL_PREF (the tie-breaking preference within an AS), MULTI_EXIT_DISC (MED, a hint to a neighbouring AS about which ingress link to prefer), and ORIGIN (how the route entered BGP: IGP, EGP, or incomplete). The global BGP routing table now exceeds 1 million IPv4 prefixes and 200,000 IPv6 prefixes, with full feeds consuming hundreds of megabytes of memory per router.
theory.why: BGP is the protocol that literally makes the internet function. Every ISP, every cloud provider (AWS, Azure, GCP), every CDN (Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly), and nearly every large enterprise with multi-homed internet connectivity runs BGP. Mastering BGP is essential for network engineering roles because: (1) Multi-homed internet connectivity requires BGP to control inbound and outbound traffic flows — if you have two ISP links, BGP lets you prefer one ISP for certain destinations and the other for the rest; (2) BGP policy control enables traffic engineering — you can manipulate Local Preference to influence outbound path selection and MED/AS_PATH prepending to influence inbound path selection; (3) BGP is the foundation of MPLS Layer 3 VPNs and EVPN fabrics in service provider and data centre networks; (4) Cloud connectivity to AWS Direct Connect, Azure ExpressRoute, and GCP Cloud Interconnect uses BGP sessions for dynamic route exchange; (5) BGP's path attribute system provides fine-grained control that no IGP can match — you cannot tell OSPF 'use link A for HTTP traffic and link B for everything else', but BGP can achieve this through communities and policy-maps. Understanding BGP convergence behaviour, route reflectors, confederations, and prefix filtering is critical for preventing both blackholing and route leaks.
theory.how: BGP operation proceeds through session establishment, route exchange, best-path selection, and ongoing maintenance. Phase 1 — Session Establishment: Two BGP peers open a TCP connection on port 179. The active (initiating) peer sends an OPEN message containing its AS number, Hold Time (default 90s), BGP identifier (router ID), and optional capabilities (multi-protocol extensions, route refresh, 4-byte AS). The receiving peer validates the AS number (for eBGP, must match the configured remote-as; for iBGP, must match the local AS), and responds with its own OPEN. Upon agreement, peers enter the Established state and send a KEEPALIVE message. Phase 2 — Initial Route Exchange: After establishment, peers exchange UPDATE messages containing all feasible routes. Each UPDATE can advertise one prefix with full path attributes and simultaneously withdraw multiple withdrawn routes. Initial exchange on the internet can involve many millions of prefixes, taking minutes to complete. Phase 3 — Incremental Updates: After the initial exchange, only changes are sent. A withdrawn route is signalled by its prefix in the withdrawn-routes field. A new or changed route is sent with the NLRI (Network Layer Reachability Information) and updated attributes. Peers also send periodic KEEPALIVE messages every 1/3 of the Hold Time (default 30s) to maintain the session. Phase 4 — Best Path Selection: BGP installs only one best path into the routing table per prefix, evaluated through a multi-step decision process: (1) Highest Weight (Cisco-proprietary, local to router), (2) Highest LOCAL_PREF (preferred eBGP exit point), (3) Locally originated routes, (4) Shortest AS_PATH, (5) Lowest ORIGIN (IGP < EGP < incomplete), (6) Lowest MED, (7) eBGP preferred over iBGP, (8) Lowest IGP metric to NEXT_HOP, (9) Oldest route (for eBGP multipath stability), (10) Lowest Router-ID. eBGP vs iBGP: eBGP runs between different ASes with TTL=1 by default, employs loop prevention through AS_PATH (rejects any update containing its own AS), and all eBGP-learned routes are advertised to both eBGP and iBGP peers by default. iBGP runs within the same AS, requires all iBGP speakers to be in a full mesh (or use route reflectors to scale), and routes learned from an iBGP peer are NOT re-advertised to other iBGP peers (the split-horizon rule that necessitates route reflectors or confederations).
theory.when: Deploy BGP in the following scenarios: (1) Multi-homed internet connectivity — when your organisation has two or more upstream ISPs, BGP lets you advertise your public prefixes (PI space) to both and control which ISP carries your inbound and outbound traffic; (2) ISP peering — IXP (Internet Exchange Point) public peering or private peering with other ISPs requires BGP; (3) Cloud on-ramp — AWS Direct Connect, Azure ExpressRoute, and GCP Cloud Interconnect all terminate in BGP sessions exchanging your VPC/VNet prefixes; (4) Data centre fabric — BGP as the underlay routing protocol in leaf-spine EVPN/VXLAN fabrics (RFC 7938) provides scalable, policy-rich routing with ECMP support across all leaf-to-spine paths; (5) MPLS VPNs — Provider Edge (PE) routers use MP-BGP (Multiprotocol BGP) with VPNv4 address families to transport customer VPN routes across the provider backbone; (6) Large enterprise WAN — organisations with hundreds of sites may run BGP internally with private AS numbers to manage complex routing policies across multiple regions or business units. Do NOT use BGP for simple internal routing where an IGP (OSPF, IS-IS) suffices — BGP adds configuration complexity, slower convergence (can be 30-90 seconds without BGP Fast External Failover or BFD), and higher operational overhead from attribute management.
key_concepts: Autonomous System (AS): unique 16-bit (1-64511) or 32-bit (65536-4294967295) identifier; private AS range 64512-65535
eBGP (External BGP): between different ASes, TTL=1, AS_PATH loop prevention, routes re-advertised freely
iBGP (Internal BGP): within same AS, requires full mesh (or route reflectors), split-horizon prevents re-advertising iBGP-learned routes
Route Reflector (RR): scales iBGP by reflecting routes to clients; avoids O(n²) full mesh requirement
AS_PATH attribute: sequence of AS numbers the route traversed; used for loop detection and path length comparison
Local Preference (LOCAL_PREF): 32-bit integer, higher preferred; advertised within AS only, controls outbound exit selection
Multi-Exit Discriminator (MED): 32-bit metric, lower preferred; exchanged between ASes, influences inbound path selection
BGP Communities: 32-bit tags for inter-AS signalling (well-known: NO_EXPORT, NO_ADVERTISE, LOCAL_AS)
Best Path Selection: 10-step decision process (Weight, Local Pref, Local origin, AS path, Origin, MED, eBGP/iBGP, IGP metric, Age, Router ID)
Prefix filtering with prefix-lists, AS_PATH access-lists, route-maps, and filtering based on communities
BGP convergence: ~90s by default (hold timer); accelerated via BFD, Fast External Failover, and session establishment optimization
BGP UPDATE message format: withdrawn routes + path attributes + NLRI

BGP path attributes: Well-known mandatory (AS_PATH, NEXT_HOP, ORIGIN), Well-known discretionary (LOCAL_PREF, ATOMIC_AGGREGATE), Optional transitive (AGGREGATOR, COMMUNITY), Optional non-transitive (MULTI_EXIT_DISC)
Multiprotocol BGP (MP-BGP): VPNv4, IPv6 (AFI 2/SAFI 1), EVPN (AFI 25/SAFI 70), VPN-IPv6 (AFI 2/SAFI 128)
BGP PIC (Prefix Independent Convergence): fast failover to backup path, uses BGP backup path calculation
BGP Flowspec: traffic filtering via BGP, DDoS mitigation by propagating filter rules across infrastructure
Graceful restart / NSF: hitless BGP session restart with forwarding state preservation
theory.configuration:
! Basic eBGP configuration
router bgp 65001
 bgp router-id 10.0.0.1
 bgp log-neighbor-changes

! eBGP neighbour (multi-homing to ISP)
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 remote-as 65002
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 description PRIMARY-ISP
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 ebgp-multihop 2
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 update-source Loopback0
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 password BGPSecure123
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 timers 10 30

! Secondary ISP with lower Local Preference for backup
 neighbor 198.51.100.1 remote-as 65003
 neighbor 198.51.100.1 description BACKUP-ISP
 neighbor 198.51.100.1 password BGPSecure456

! Advertise local prefixes into BGP
 network 10.0.0.0 mask 255.255.0.0
 network 192.168.0.0 mask 255.255.0.0

! Set Local Preference via route-map for traffic engineering
 route-map SET-LOCAL-PREF permit 10
 set local-preference 150
! Apply to updates FROM PRIMARY ISP
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 route-map SET-LOCAL-PREF in

! Prefix filtering to reject bogons
 ip prefix-list ALLOWED-PREFIXES permit 10.0.0.0/8 le 24
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 prefix-list ALLOWED-PREFIXES in
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 prefix-list ALLOWED-PREFIXES out

! iBGP full mesh with route reflectors
 neighbor 10.0.0.2 remote-as 65001
 neighbor 10.0.0.2 description R2-iBGP
 neighbor 10.0.0.2 update-source Loopback0
! This router acts as a route reflector
 neighbor 10.0.0.2 route-reflector-client
troubleshooting: show ip bgp summary — Quick peer status: Established count, prefixes received, state per peer
show ip bgp [prefix] — Detailed route attributes, path selection tiebreaker steps
show ip bgp neighbors [addr] — Full session details: state, timers, capabilities, version, prefixes
show ip bgp neighbors [addr] received-routes — What BGP has received (requires soft-reconfiguration inbound)
show ip bgp neighbors [addr] advertised-routes — What BGP is advertising outbound
show ip bgp rib-failure — Routes that BGP knows but did not install in RIB (typically due to admin distance or metric)
show ip route bgp — BGP-originated routes in the routing table
show bgp ipv4 unicast summary — IPv4 AF-specific peer summary (useful in MP-BGP scenarios)
debug ip bgp updates — Log BGP UPDATE messages (caution: high output on busy peers)
ping 203.0.113.1 source Loopback0 — Verify TCP reachability to the BGP neighbour
traceroute 203.0.113.1 source Loopback0 — Verify BGP multi-hop path (for eBGP multihop)
show ip bgp community — Inspect routes tagged with specific BGP communities

theory.what: HSRP and VRRP provide gateway redundancy — if the primary router fails, a backup takes over the virtual IP seamlessly. Clients never need to change their default gateway.
theory.why: A single router as default gateway is a single point of failure. FHRP ensures continuous connectivity even when a router fails — essential for high availability.
theory.how:
HSRP/VRRP create a virtual IP shared between routers:
- Active/Master router responds to the virtual IP
- Standby/Backup monitors via hello packets
- If Active fails, Standby takes over (typically 3-10 seconds)
- Clients configured with virtual IP as gateway

HSRP: Cisco proprietary. VRRP: Open standard (RFC 5798).
theory.when: Use FHRP whenever you have redundant routers/L3 switches serving as default gateways. Required for any HA network design.
key_concepts: Virtual IP (VIP)
Active/Standby (HSRP) or Master/Backup (VRRP)
Priority (higher = preferred)
Preemption
Hello/Hold timers
Interface tracking
theory.configuration:
! HSRP
interface Vlan10
 ip address 10.0.10.2 255.255.255.0
 standby 1 ip 10.0.10.1
 standby 1 priority 110
 standby 1 preempt
 standby 1 track GigabitEthernet0/0
troubleshooting: show standby
show standby brief
show vrrp
debug standby

theory.what: EtherChannel bundles multiple physical links into one logical link, providing increased bandwidth and redundancy without STP blocking the extra links.
theory.why: STP blocks redundant links. EtherChannel tricks STP into seeing multiple links as one, so all links are active. Doubles/triples bandwidth while providing failover.
theory.how:
Negotiation protocols:
- LACP (802.3ad): Open standard, preferred
- PAgP: Cisco proprietary
- Static: No negotiation (not recommended)

All member links must have same speed, duplex, VLAN, and trunk settings.
theory.when: Use EtherChannel between switches, between switch and server, or between switch and router when you need more bandwidth than a single link provides.
key_concepts: LACP (active/passive)
PAgP (desirable/auto)
Load balancing (src-mac, dst-mac, src-dst-ip)
All links must match settings
Port-channel interface
Maximum 8 links per channel
theory.configuration:
! LACP EtherChannel
interface range GigabitEthernet0/1-2
 channel-group 1 mode active
!
interface Port-channel1
 switchport mode trunk
troubleshooting: show etherchannel summary
show etherchannel port-channel
show lacp neighbor
show pagp neighbor

theory.what: QoS prioritizes certain traffic types over others when network congestion occurs. It ensures critical applications (voice, video) get bandwidth while less important traffic waits.
theory.why: Without QoS, all traffic is treated equally. During congestion, voice calls drop, video freezes, and critical apps slow down. QoS ensures business-critical traffic always gets through.
theory.how:
QoS mechanisms:
1. Classification: Identify traffic (DSCP, ACL, NBAR)
2. Marking: Tag packets with priority (DSCP values)
3. Queuing: Place in priority queues
4. Scheduling: Serve queues (strict priority, weighted fair)
5. Policing/Shaping: Limit bandwidth

Trust boundaries: Where markings are accepted.
theory.when: Implement QoS when: running VoIP, video conferencing, or any real-time application over a shared network. Also for WAN links with limited bandwidth.
key_concepts: DSCP (Differentiated Services Code Point)
Classification and Marking
Queuing (LLQ, CBWFQ)
Policing vs Shaping
Trust boundary
EF (Expedited Forwarding) for voice
theory.configuration:
! Classify and mark voice
class-map match-all VOICE
 match protocol rtp
policy-map QOS-POLICY
 class VOICE
  priority 256
 class class-default
  fair-queue
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 service-policy output QOS-POLICY
troubleshooting: show policy-map interface
show class-map
show mls qos interface
show queuing
